full_judgment:
Mohammad Abdul Khaliq, J: This rule was issued calling upon the opposite party to show cause why the judgment and order passed by the learned S.C.C. Judge in S.C. Suit No.8 of 1978 decreeing the suit should not be set aside. 

 4. The learned S.C.C. Judge held that the defendant is a defaulter that defendant No.1 has sublet the premises to defendant No. 2 and on those grounds he decreed the suit for ejectment and also for recovery of Taka 237/80 as arrear rent. 

 10. Mr. F. Karim, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff opposite party submits that although the claim was for Taka 1142/- as arrear rent in the suit, the trial Court decreed the suit only for Taka 237/80 and as such the decree passed by the court below is within the pecuniary jurisdiction of the S. C. Court. He further submits that section 11 of the Suit Valuation Act applies in this case. As the decision has not prejudicially affected the merit of the case owing to over-valuation the judgment and order passed by the court below cannot be interfered with. He has referred to the decision in the case of Kiran Singh arid others vs Chaman Pachawan and others reported in A.I.R. 1954 SC page 340 in support of his submission that the policy underlying section 21 and section 99 of the C.P.C and section 11 of the Suit Valuation Act is the same, namely, that when a case bad been tried by a court on merit and judgment rendered, it should not be liable to be reversed purely on technical grounds, unless it has resulted in the failure of justice, and the policy of the legislature has been to treat objections to jurisdiction both territorial and pecuniary as technical and not open to consideration by an appellate court unless there has been prejudice on the merits. 

 13. Mr. B.K. Das submits that section 11 of the Suit Valuation Act does not apply as it is, a suit under Small Cause Court Act and the pecuniary jurisdiction or the Small Cause Court has been fixed by section 15 of Small Cause Court Act. The limit of pecuniary jurisdiction has undoubtedly been fixed by section 15(2) of the S C Court Act. But fixation of pecuniary jurisdiction by Statute is one thing and the procedure to value a suit is another thing. The procedure how a suit should be valued has been prescribed in the Suit Valuation Act. Part I of the Suit Valuation Act applies to the case of suits relating to land. Part II relates to other suits. Section 8 provides that in suits other than those referred to in Court Fees Act section 7, paragraphs V. VI and IX and paragraph X clause (c), court fees are payable ad-valorem under Court Fees Act, the value as determinable for computation of court fees and the value for the purpose of jurisdiction shall be the same. So, according to section 8, the value determined for Court fees in those suits would also be the valuation for the purpose of jurisdiction of those suits. Para 1 of section 7 of the Court Fees Act provides the procedure for computation of fees in a suit for money and section 7 para 11 (CC) provides for computation of court fees in suit for recovery of immovable property from the tenant after the determination of the tenancy. According to section 8 of the Suit Valuation Act, therefore, provision has been made how a suit should be valued for the purpose of jurisdiction in the case of the present nature, It cannot, therefore, be said that section 11, does not apply in the present case. In connection with section 11, Mr. Das submits that as jurisdiction of the court is affected in this case so provision of section 99 applies. The provision of section 99 of the C.P.C. is that no decree shall be reversed or modified for error, defect or irregularity not affecting the merit or jurisdiction. Section 99 C.P.C. applies where the error, defect or irregularity it the proceed in has affected the merit of the case or jurisdiction. The submission of Mr. Das therefore appears to be correct. But section 11 of the suit valuation overrides the provision of section 99 C.P.C. in respect of jurisdiction on certain conditions as mentioned above. Again the object of section 99 of the Code of Civil Procedure and section l1 of Suit Valuation Act appears to be same i.e. judgment should not be disturbed on technical ground. This view finds support from the decision in the case reported in A.I.R. 1954 (SC) page 340 referred to above. Section 11, as has been mentioned above, provides that if the suit is overvalued or undervalued and, if no objection was taken before the trial court or appellate courting the present case there was no appeal, so the question of appellate court judgment dose not arise) no such objection can be raised at a later stage. Mr. B. K. Das submits that he has no objection with regard to valuation of suit. He rather submits that plaintiff correctly valued the suit but the small cause court has no jurisdiction to take cognizance of the suit as the suit was beyond pecuniary jurisdiction of court. The question of jurisdiction, in the present case about pecuniary jurisdiction, will have to be decided on the basis of the amount at which the plaintiff valued the suit. Plaintiff has given valuation of the suit as Taka 1430/- for the purpose of pecuniary jurisdiction and on the basis of it the court had to decide whether it had pecuniary jurisdiction.to entertain the suit. Admittedly the court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. But in fact it entertained the suit and decided it on merit without any objection. It does not appear that the error to entertain the suit which was beyond the pecuniary jurisdiction of the court has prejudicially affected the disposal of the suit on merit. When no objections in this re are WAS taken before the trial court it cannot be entertained in this Revisional case in the above circumstances. The objection cannot also be entertained at this stage under section 21 of the Code of Civil Procedure as the objection was not taken in the trial Court and as there has been no failure of justice. In such circumstances I do not find any ground to interfere with the judgment and order passed by the trial court.
